extracted.intended_audience: laypersons providing first aid / general public
extracted.subtask_description: Practical first-aid instructions and diagnostic signs for common soft-tissue injuries, foreign bodies, and fractures aimed at lay responders to stabilize patients, relieve pain, prevent infection, and obtain surgical help when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of bruises
rubrics_metrics.description: Even slight and moderate bruises should be treated by rest of the injured part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Snug application of a flannel bandage to secure rest and prevent further swelling; when bandaging not feasible use cold compress: one layer of thin cotton or linen wet in ice water and continually renewed. Alcohol and water (equal parts) may be used similarly. If cold is unavailable or unpleasant, apply several layers of cotton cloth wrung out in very hot water with frequent renewal. Cataplasma Kaolini is recommended when spread thickly and covered with bandage; an ointment with 25% ichthyol is useful. Following severe bruises keep parts warm with hot-water bags or cotton wool until surgical advice obtained. As pain and swelling subside, rub with liniment of ammonia or chloroform (or vaseline if unavailable) and begin moderate exercise of the part.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of abrasions
rubrics_metrics.description: When the surface skin is scraped off (abrasion), use an ointment containing boric acid in vaseline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ointment: sixty grains of boric acid to the ounce of vaseline; apply and cover with a bandage. The same ointment is useful on small wounds and cuts after the first bandage is removed.

rubrics_metrics.name: First aid for sprain (no displacement of bones)
rubrics_metrics.description: Immediate simple measures for sprains: hot immersion, immobilization/strapping, and rest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First Aid Rule 1: Immerse in water as hot as the hand can bear for half an hour. Rule 2: Dry and strap with adhesive plaster if skilled; if not, bandage snugly beginning at fingertips or toes and apply uniform pressure. Rule 3: Rest; if ankle or knee is hurt, patient must go to bed. Do not use these methods except in slight unmistakable sprains or until a surgeon is available. Beware of confusing severe sprain with dislocation or fracture—seek surgical aid when there is inability to move joint and great swelling. After initial hot immersion, apply an elastic flannel bandage (cut on the bias ~3½ inches wide) starting at tips and carrying above the joint. Avoid over-tight bandaging—remove and reapply if numbness, coldness, or blueness appear. For ankle/knee, bed rest at least 24 hours; for wrist/shoulder use a sling; splint before bandaging in more serious cases. For ordinary ankle sprains: after day 1 alternate immersion (hot 5 minutes / cold 5 minutes), followed by gentle rubbing with chloroform liniment (not touching joint initially), increasing vigor gradually, once daily, then bandage; moderate use regained in 2–3 weeks. More severe sprains may require plaster-of-Paris splinting by a surgeon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing sprain, dislocation, and fracture
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether injury is sprain, dislocation, rupture, or fracture; treatment differs accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sprain produces temporary displacement sufficient to damage soft structures but not lasting bone displacement. Severe sprain with inability to move, great swelling, or signs inconsistent with simple sprain should prompt surgical evaluation. Since X-ray can reveal breaks not detectable by older methods, assume severe injuries may be fractures and seek surgical aid before attempting definitive treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: First aid for synovitis (severe joint injury; 'water on the knee')
rubrics_metrics.description: Treatment for synovitis from wrench, blow, or fall—commonly knee, ankle, elbow, hip.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First Aid Rule 1: Alternate pouring hot and cold water over the joint (hot, return to pitcher, cold, return; repeat hot then cold) for half an hour. Rule 2: Put to bed with hot-water bottles about the joint and wedge immovably with pillows. Rule 3: When tenderness and heat subside, strap with adhesive plaster in overlapping strips. If knee is red, hot, or tender, apply a splint and keep patient in bed until symptoms subside. Splint options: heavy pasteboard wet and covered with wadding from six inches below to four inches above joint, secured with adhesive plaster and bandage; padded wooden splint also acceptable. For mild cases or after acute tenderness abates, a pad behind the knee plus encasing adhesive plaster 'garters' from five inches below to four inches above the joint, then a cotton bandage, allows the patient to walk without bending the knee. When swelling has nearly departed, remove plaster and begin twice-daily rubbing and passive movement by attendant; paint spots of knee with tincture of iodine; do not bend knee in walking until it can be moved by another person without discomfort. When a physician can be obtained, laymen should not attempt to treat severe cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of bunion and housemaid's knee (bursal swellings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Manage acute painful bursitis of the great toe (bunion) and prepatellar bursa (housemaid's knee).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acute painful cases: absolute rest with foot elevated; apply cloths kept constantly wet with ice or cold water, or a thick Cataplasma Kaolini until inflammation subsides. If chronic or unresponsive, consult a surgeon—may require incision and drainage for abscess. For milder bunions, wear proper shoes (inner border straight from heel to toe) and paint with tincture of iodine every few days until skin becomes sore.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of run-around; whitlow or felon (finger infections)
rubrics_metrics.description: Early management of soft-tissue infections around fingernail (paronychia/run-around) and deep palmar felon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Run-around: treat with iodine, cold applications, and if inflammation continues, hot poulticing and incision; poulticing often sufficient. Felon: at outset, keep finger constantly wet with bandage saturated with equal parts alcohol and water; at night cover with oil silk or rubber; paint with tincture of iodine; keep hand elevated in sling. If pain increases after 24 hours apply hot poultices frequently; if no abatement by 48 hours, surgical incision cutting lengthwise to the bone is indicated to prevent bone death or extension of infection. Seek attention to general health from a physician as helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Management of weeping sinew (ganglion)
rubrics_metrics.description: A non-painful cystic swelling on dorsum or volar wrist containing gelatinous substance in a sac.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treatment: sudden great pressure on the swelling with the thumb or a sharp blow with a book to rupture the sac so contents escape and are usually absorbed. If swelling recurs, a slight surgical operation will permanently cure the trouble. Note: usually not red or inflamed and may persist indefinitely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal of foreign bodies from the eye
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedure for removing cinders or foreign bodies lodged under upper lid or on eyeball surface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A drop of 2% cocaine anesthetic may be used. Direct patient to look downward; grasp lashes and lid edge with forefinger and thumb of right hand, press a small pencil against upper part of the lid and lift lower part outward and upward over the pencil to evert the lid; keep it in position and gently sweep offending body off the mucous membrane with a fold of soft, clean handkerchief. Use blotting-paper for removal if possible. Refer all deep or embedded hot cinders/metal fragments promptly to a physician; laymen should not use needles or instruments unless no medical aid for days and done carefully. After removal, if considerable irritation occurred, instill boric acid solution (10 grains to ounce of water) four times daily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Management of foreign bodies in the ear
rubrics_metrics.description: How to deal with solid objects and insects in the ear canal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insects: kill by dropping sweet oil, castor, linseed, machine oil, glycerin, or even water, then remove after ~30 minutes by syringing warm water. For solid smooth objects, turn ear downward, pull it outward and backward and rub skin in front of opening to encourage object to fall out. If this fails, syringing with warm water while patient sits may work. Avoid unskillful instrumental attempts; if syringing fails, await skilled medical services. For seeds/beans that may swell, place glycerin to absorb water and shrink the seed before syringing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Management of foreign bodies in the nose
rubrics_metrics.description: Removal attempts for nostril foreign bodies, especially in children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If visible, close the unobstructed nostril and have the child blow out of the affected side. If blowing fails or the object not visible, seek medical aid promptly. Be alert for thick foul-smelling discharge from one nostril as a sign of retained foreign body.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to tell a broken bone (diagnosis of fracture)
rubrics_metrics.description: Clinical signs to determine whether a bone is broken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First Aid Rule 1: Be sure bone is broken. If broken, patient can scarcely (if at all) move the part beyond the break, while attendant can move it freely in his hands. If broken, grating of rough edges of bone may be felt by attendant but should not be sought for. If broken, limb is generally shortened. Other absolute tests: unusual mobility in the course of the bone and grating of the broken fragments together. Sudden shortening from overlap is also a sure sign. Do not seek grating deliberately. First Aid Rule 2: Do not try to set bone permanently. Send at once for surgeon.

rubrics_metrics.name: First aid for compound fracture (prevent infection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Immediate measures when a fracture opens to the air (compound) to reduce infection risk and save life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Important: before reducing fracture and without much movement of the patient, scrub hands very clean. First Aid Rule 1: If hairy, shave large spot about wound. Rule 2: Clean a large area about wound gently with soap and water, then wash thoroughly with previously boiled and cooled water; flood the wound with cool boiled water. Rule 3: Cover wound with absorbent cotton or boiled muslin. Then attend to immobilization of broken bone. After bone is set: Rule 4: Renew boiled muslin when stained; every day wash carefully about wound between splints with cool carbolic-acid solution (one teaspoonful to a pint of hot water) before putting on fresh cloths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles of immediate fracture care
rubrics_metrics.description: Overall aims and principles for first treatment of fractures by lay responders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate treatment is not essential to the bone's union (which takes weeks) but is vital to prevent pain and avoid further damage from sharp bone ends injuring soft tissues. Keep the limb quiet in a fair position until surgeon sees it. Understand fracture classifications (partial/complete, simple/compound) and use tests (inability to use limb, deformity, unusual mobility, grating) to distinguish from sprain or bruise. Handle patient with utmost gentleness.

rubrics_metrics.name: First aid for broken rib
rubrics_metrics.description: Immediate immobilization and pain relief for suspected rib fracture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First Aid Rule: Patient places hands on head while attendant applies adhesive-plaster band one foot wide around injured side from spine over breastbone to line of armpit of sound side; then put patient to bed. Method: overlap strips 4–5 inches wide until 1 foot width obtained, stick one end along backbone and carry forward around injured side to just below armpit of uninjured side. If surgeon's plaster unavailable, use a strong unbleached cotton or flannel bandage a foot wide secured with safety pins to limit chest motion. Patient may be more comfortable sitting up. Avoid exposure to cold or wet as pleurisy/pneumonia may follow. Firm union in ~3 weeks.

rubrics_metrics.name: First aid for collar-bone (clavicle) fracture
rubrics_metrics.description: Positioning and support for clavicle fracture to ensure rest and alignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First Aid Rule: Put patient flat on back on a level bed with small pillow between shoulders; place forearm of injured side across chest and retain with bandage about chest and arm. Alternative: sling to raise and support shoulder when patient ambulates (less wearisome than prolonged recumbency). To make a sling: cut cotton cloth a yard square diagonally to form triangles; support hand and forearm. In children clavicle fractures often are green-stick (partial) and require less intervention.

rubrics_metrics.name: First aid for lower-jaw (mandible) fracture
rubrics_metrics.description: Temporary reduction and immobilization of mandibular fragments and feeding precautions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First Aid Rule: Put fragments into place with fingers securing good line of the teeth. Support lower jaw by firmly bandaging it against upper jaw, mouth shut, using a four-tailed bandage. Feeding is done through a glass tube using milk, broths, thin gruels. Use mouth wash four times daily to keep mouth clean and aid gum healing (menthol ½ grain, thymol ½ grain, boric acid 20 grains in 8 oz water).

rubrics_metrics.name: First aid for shoulder-blade (scapula) fracture
rubrics_metrics.description: Immobilize arm and shoulder to prevent displacement of scapular fracture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First Aid Rule: There is usually no displacement. Bandage fingers, forearm, and arm of affected side and put the arm in a sling. Fasten slung arm to body with many turns of a bandage, holding forearm against chest and arm against side. Use straps over shoulders attached to the bandage to prevent slipping.

rubrics_metrics.name: First aid for arm fracture (humerus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduction by traction, padding, splinting, and support for fractures between shoulder and elbow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First Aid Rule: Pad two thin boards (~9x3 inches) with handkerchiefs. Carefully pull fragments apart by grasping lower fragment near elbow while assistant pulls on upper near shoulder. Place padded splints one each side of fracture and wind bandage along whole length tightly enough to hold fragments firm. Put forearm and hand in a sling. Additional measures: bandage hand and forearm from below upward to elbow; place wedge-shaped pad from armpit to elbow to maintain position (pad held by adhesive plaster or bandage); apply three well-padded thin boards against front, outside, and back of arm secured by plaster/bandage; bring arm into pad and encase with wide bandage around arm and chest from shoulder to elbow and straps over shoulders; wrist supported in sling, forearm horizontal. Firm union in 4–6 weeks.

rubrics_metrics.name: First aid for forearm fracture
rubrics_metrics.description: Basic setting by traction and splinting for fractures of the forearm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First Aid Rule: Set bones in proper place by pulling steadily on the wrist while an assistant holds the upper part of the forearm. Then apply appropriate splints and bandaging as for other limb fractures. (Detailed splinting instructions continue beyond this chunk.)
